paragraphs.heading: What the Paleozoic is
paragraphs.text: The Paleozoic is the earliest of the three eras that make up the Phanerozoic Eon. It began 538.8 million years ago, taking over from the Neoproterozoic, and closed 251.902 million years ago when the Mesozoic Era started. Geologists split it into six periods; oldest first, they are the Cambrian, Ordovician, Silurian, Devonian, Carboniferous and Permian. Some timescales also group the first three as an Early Paleozoic and the last three as a Late Paleozoic, though this split is informal.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: The word is built from Greek roots and means "ancient life". Adam Sedgwick first used it in 1838 for just the Cambrian and Ordovician periods. In 1840 John Phillips stretched it to run from the Cambrian all the way to the Permian.

paragraphs.heading: Life fills the seas and the land
paragraphs.text: The era brought sweeping change to rocks, climate and living things. The Cambrian saw the Cambrian explosion, the quickest and broadest spread of new life in Earth's history, when most of today's phyla (basic body plans) first showed up. Arthropods, molluscs, fish, amphibians, reptiles and synapsids all arose during the era. Life started out in the ocean and later moved onto land, and by the late Paleozoic vast forests of early plants covered the continents; many of those forests became the coal beds of Europe and eastern North America.

paragraphs.heading: How the start is marked
paragraphs.text: The base of the Paleozoic is one of the big dividing lines in geologic time. Sedgwick placed it at the first sign of complex life in the rocks, shown by fossil groups dominated by trilobites. Later, the first small shelly fossils became the marker, but most rock sequences from that time are of a kind in which skeletal fossils rarely survive. So the International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS) turned to trace fossils, which reflect how complex the body of the maker was, and which grew more varied and complex as more complex organisms evolved.

paragraphs.heading: A reference point in Newfoundland
paragraphs.text: After twenty years of debate, the ICS picked Fortune Head on the Burin Peninsula of Newfoundland as the official reference point for the start of the Cambrian. It sits at the base of a group of trace fossils called Treptichnus pedum. That level is dated at 538.8 ± 0.6 million years ago, which puts it below the first trilobites and the first small shelly fossils.

paragraphs.heading: Continents on the move
paragraphs.text: The era opened as the supercontinent Pannotia broke apart, a breakup that began with the opening of the Iapetus Ocean and came with a sharp rise in sea level. The large continent Gondwana then came together, about 510 million years ago. By the middle of the era, North America and Europe had collided, raising the Acadian-Caledonian uplifts. Late in the era, more collisions built the supercontinent Pangaea along with great mountain chains such as the Appalachians and the Urals.

paragraphs.heading: How the era ended
paragraphs.text: The Paleozoic closed with the Permian–Triassic extinction, the largest extinction event of the whole Phanerozoic Eon. The damage was so severe that life on land needed 30 million years, well into the Mesozoic, to recover, while sea life may have bounced back much faster. Today the boundary is set by the first appearance of Hindeodus parvus, a conodont, at a site near Meishan in southern China. Dating of volcanic clay layers just above and below it pins its age to 251.902 ± 0.024 million years ago.
